Chapter 13 · Spatial Intelligence for Intelligent Assistance

13.3Pivotal Task-1: Managing the Physical Environment

PDF p. 437· 3 min read

The most autonomous regime asks the assistant to maintain the physical state of a human environment with little real-time supervision. A persistent model of the dwelling supports two complementary operations: grounding instructions for physical action, and retrieving remembered evidence to answer queries. New observations update the model, including after an action changes the environment. Figure 13.2 separates these action and recall branches around their shared home memory.

Representing the home. Everything downstream depends on a queryable model of the space, which extends the scene-understanding methods of Chapter 6 into a persistent, semantically indexed memory. The memory architectures themselves are treated in Section 7.3.6; here they are the infrastructure that lets an assistant know not only where surfaces are, but what and whose. The 3D scene graph [333] introduced a hierarchical structure that unifies objects, rooms, and cameras with the underlying geometry, and Hydra [1541] brought such graphs into real-time, loop-closure-optimized robot perception so that the memory stays current as the assistant moves. To make the memory addressable by free-form language, ConceptFusion [2922] builds an open-set, multimodal 3D map that answers text, image, or click queries, and ConceptGraphs [1542] fuses foundation-model outputs across views into a captioned, language-queryable 3D scene graph suitable for planning. This open-vocabulary memory is what lets an assistant act on objects it was never explicitly trained to recognize.

Acting on the space: tidy-up and rearrangement. Restoring order is the canonical management task, framed by Batra et al.[2923] as bringing an environment from an arbitrary configuration into a target spatial state. The benchmark substrate includes the Visual Room Rearrangement (RoomR) challenge [2924], which asks an agent to observe a goal arrangement and then reset one to five displaced objects, and Housekeep [2925], which removes the explicit goal and instead judges placements against human preferences over nearly two thousand objects. Method work has moved from fixed rules to learned commonsense priors. TIDEE [2926] tidies a never-before-seen room from pixels using a visuo-semantic out-of-place detector and an associative memory of where receptacles tend to be, and TidyBot [2927] makes the placement preference-aware, using few-shot summarization with a large language model to generalize a particular user’s tidying rules from a handful of examples. The shift these systems mark, from a universal notion of tidiness to one conditioned on the resident, is exactly the personalization property that defines the assistant.

Acting on the space: open-vocabulary mobile manipulation. Tidying a real home requires picking and placing arbitrary objects at arbitrary locations, the task formalized as open-vocabulary mobile manipulation by HomeRobot [2928], which pairs a simulation and real benchmark with a software stack for the Hello Robot Stretch. Notable deployment evidence comes from OK-Robot [2929], which combines a phone-scanned dense vision-language map with off-the-shelf navigation and grasping to achieve zero-shot pick-and-drop across ten real homes, and from Mobile ALOHA [2930], which shows that low-cost whole-body teleoperation plus imitation learning can acquire dexterous bimanual household skills. These systems lean directly on the manipulation primitives of Section 9.1, increasingly instantiated as generalist vision-language-action policies (e.g., , OpenVLA [98], π0\pi_{0} [99]) that fold perception, grounding, and control into one model; the assistant contribution is to drive them in unstructured homes from open-vocabulary goals rather than in an engineered cell. Commercial and pre-commercial examples illustrate the same pressure from different directions: mapping vacuum robots such as iRobot’s Roomba, which build semantic room maps for targeted cleaning,1 represent the mature narrow end, while emerging home-humanoid platforms such as 1X’s Neo2 and Figure3 show how the field is attempting, so far without a general-purpose result, to generalize mobile manipulation into domestic settings.

Searching and recalling the model. The dual of acting on the space is querying it: an assistant is, among other things, a search engine for the physical world that answers “where did I leave my keys?” Object-goal navigation supplies the active half, with goal-oriented semantic exploration (SemExp) [1404] building an episodic semantic map and a policy that exploits object co-occurrence to find a target efficiently rather than searching blindly. Embodied question answering [1392] couples navigation with answering, and its open-vocabulary successor OpenEQA [1550] spans both an episodic-memory setting, in which the assistant must recall what it has already seen, and an active-exploration setting, over more than a hundred real environments. For wearable assistants that record the user’s day, the same recall problem becomes natural-language search of long egocentric video, the episodic-memory task defined by Ego4D [673]. This is the application-facing counterpart of the memory-augmented reasoning systems in Section 7.3.6.
